Essential Takeaways


- Connected technologies are helping washing machines make smarter decisions with less consumer effort.
- Collaboration among chemistry, appliances and digital intelligence is improving cleaning performance and resource efficiency.
- AI’s greatest impact may be making laundry technology simpler and more intuitive to use.


The relationship among detergents, appliances and consumers is becoming more dynamic. Advances in sensing technology, automation and connectivity are allowing washing machines to respond to each load in real time, improving cleaning performance while using water, energy and detergent more efficiently. Artificial intelligence is accelerating that evolution, but its greatest impact may be making the technology itself less visible.


### Smarter Machines


Today’s washing machines do much more than execute a programmed cycle. Many automatically detect load size, fabric type and soil level, adjusting water levels, cycle length and detergent dosage to match each wash. Bosch’s ActiveWater Plus, for example, detects 256 load levels to measure water more precisely, while i-DOS systems dispense detergent automatically to help avoid overdosing and unnecessary rinsing. LG’s AI DD technology analyzes load weight and fabric softness to select wash motions designed to improve fabric care.


Across Bosch, LG and other​​ ​​major appliance brands: a common approach is emerging: sensor-driven water dosing, smarter spray or circulation systems and automatic detergent dosing. Some systems claim water savings of roughly 20% per cycle. The common thread is not adding more features. It is using the right amount of water, energy and detergent for each load.

### A Connected Laundry Ecosystem


Smarter appliances are also changing how different parts of the laundry ecosystem work together. Rather than developing detergents and machines independently, manufacturers are increasingly collaborating to ensure formulations, appliance technologies and wash programs complement one another.


That collaboration is becoming more important as cold-water washing gains momentum. Making cold wash work at scale requires time, temperature, chemistry, mechanical action and water to work together. Auto-dosing and “mixing-in-the-moment” technologies can also improve cold-wash performance by releasing different cleaning ingredients at the right point in the cycle.


Connectivity supports that shift. Connected appliances can monitor detergent use, adjust programs and create opportunities to improve performance throughout the appliance’s life rather than relying only on fixed settings.


> “AI shouldn’t make laundry more complicated. Its job is to quietly remove the guesswork so consumers can trust the machine to do the right thing.”


Tycho Lamberigts Senior Application Specialist at IFF, AI


### What Role Could AI Play?


For Tycho Lamberigts, Senior Application Specialist at IFF, AI is most valuable when consumers barely notice it is there. The goal is not to give people more settings to manage. It is to remove friction from everyday decisions.


“Consumers should be able to push a button and walk away,” he says.


Rather than asking users to choose the right cycle, water level or detergent dosage, intelligent systems can increasingly make those decisions automatically based on sensor data and previous usage patterns. ​​Lamberigts adds, “AI shouldn’t make laundry more complicated. Its job is to quietly remove the guesswork so consumers can trust the machine to do the right thing.”


At recent consumer technology exhibitions, Lamberigts saw AI everywhere, but he also noted that adoption in appliances will be gradual because consumers do not replace washing machines every few years. That makes the near-term opportunity practical rather than futuristic: better cycle selection, smarter dosing and more responsive machines that help consumers get reliable results with less effort.


The technology is still evolving. Today’s systems can optimize wash conditions based on available data, but future generations may go further, learning from outcomes and continuously improving recommendations. The greatest value may come not from replacing people, but from quietly supporting them.


> ### The Laundry Lens
>
>
> Laundry is shifting from product performance to system performance. As laundry technologies become more connected, manufacturers will need to understand how chemistry, appliances and digital intelligence affect one another. Appliances increasingly help set the conditions for cleaning by managing water, dosing and cycle selection. Yet newer machines do not automatically lead consumers to use advanced cycles; most still rely on the Standard or Automatic setting. The opportunity is to build intelligence into the default experience, helping the system deliver better performance and resource efficiency without requiring more effort from consumers.


### What’s Next?


This issue explored how manufacturers are balancing resources and embracing smarter technologies. In our next issue, we’ll look at how changing consumer expectations and regional market dynamics are shaping the future of laundry.


- *Source: IFF, based on A.I.S.E., A compilation of life cycle studies for six household detergent product categories in Europe.*
